rendered: The documents do not test a sodium-ion electrolyte in a lithium-ion battery. Every sodium electrolyte they describe is used in a sodium cell. In a sodium sulfur study, coin cells were assembled using NaPF6 salts dissolved in tetraglyme as electrolyte[1], instead of traditional carbonate electrolytes. In an anode-free sodium study, the electrolyte was used as the electrolyte due to its stability against sodium metal[2]. The conventional lithium-ion electrolyte is described differently: Electrolyte systems in LIBs are typically made of a lithium salt, LiPF6[3], dissolved in linear carbonate solvents. A sodium salt supplies sodium ions, so a sodium electrolyte as written would not supply the lithium ions a lithium-ion cell needs. The papers also explain why sodium chemistry does not transfer directly to lithium cells: graphite, the standard lithium-ion anode, cannot intercalate sufficient sodium ions[4]. The documents also note that sodium metal is less stable with carbonate electrolytes than[5] lithium metal. So the documents do not support swapping a sodium electrolyte into a lithium-ion battery. Any such swap would need a lithium salt and a compatible electrolyte, which the documents do not evaluate.
